city.name: Berlin
summary: In July 1945 the four victors split the ruined capital into sectors: American, British and French in the west, Soviet in the east. The three western sectors became West Berlin, an island some 150 km inside the Soviet zone.

In 1948 and 1949 the Soviets blockaded West Berlin and the Western Allies kept it alive by air. On 13 August 1961 East Germany sealed the border with barbed wire, then concrete. For 28 years the Wall split streets and families, and at least 140 people were killed at it.
Scrub the timeline to watch the sectors appear, the Wall go up and come down, and the landmarks of the divided city. The Wall opened on 9 November 1989; Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.
city.note: Sector boundaries are drawn from today's Berlin district (Ortsteil) boundaries, which follow the 1945 borough lines closely; West-Staaken is cut from the British sector, but smaller exchanges of land are not shown, and the exclave of Steinstücken appears joined to Wannsee as it has been since 1972. The Wall follows the OpenStreetMap trace of its former course; the death strip is drawn as a band 85 m wide behind the inner-city Wall. Landmark positions are from Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap. properties.name: Soviet sector
properties.description: The Soviet sector: the old centre around Mitte, with Prenzlauer Berg, Friedrichshain, Pankow, Weißensee, Lichtenberg, Treptow and Köpenick. It became East Berlin, which the German Democratic Republic made its capital in 1949. The Western Allies never accepted that status.

properties.name: American sector
properties.description: The American sector: Zehlendorf, Steglitz, Schöneberg, Tempelhof, Kreuzberg and Neukölln. US troops moved in on 4 July 1945. It held Tempelhof airport, the RIAS radio station and Rathaus Schöneberg, seat of West Berlin's government.

properties.name: British sector
properties.description: The British sector: Tiergarten, Charlottenburg, Wilmersdorf and Spandau. It held the Reichstag, the Olympic Stadium, RAF Gatow and Spandau Prison, where the four powers jointly guarded Nazi war criminals.

properties.name: French sector
properties.description: The French sector: Wedding and Reinickendorf in the north. Britain handed it to France on 12 August 1945. Tegel airfield, built during the Airlift, lay here.

properties.name: British sector (later French)
properties.description: Wedding and Reinickendorf were first occupied by the British. They became the French sector on 12 August 1945, once France had been given a share of Berlin.

properties.name: Havel
properties.description: The river Havel widens into a chain of lakes along the western edge of the city. Most of the Berlin stretch lay in the British and American sectors, and the border with East Germany ran through the water in places.

properties.name: Großer Wannsee
properties.description: A bay of the Havel in the American sector, with West Berlin's lakeside beach, the Strandbad Wannsee. For West Berliners walled into their city, the lakes and forests here were the nearest open country.

properties.name: Tegeler See
properties.description: A lake on the Havel in the French sector, next to Tegel airfield.

properties.name: Müggelsee
properties.description: Berlin's largest lake, in Köpenick in the Soviet sector. It was a favourite place for East Berliners to swim and sail.

properties.name: Spree
properties.description: The river that runs through the heart of Berlin. Between Kreuzberg and Friedrichshain the whole width of the river belonged to East Berlin, so the water itself was the border.

properties.name: Landwehrkanal
properties.description: A 19th-century canal through Kreuzberg, Neukölln and Tiergarten, entirely in West Berlin. Its eastern end met the Spree at the border by the Oberbaum Bridge.

properties.name: Teltowkanal
properties.description: A shipping canal along the southern edge of the city. In several places the Wall ran along its bank.

properties.name: Berlin Wall (inner-city border)
properties.description: On 13 August 1961 East German troops sealed the border with barbed wire, and within days began replacing it with concrete; the last version, from 1975, was made of 3.6 m concrete segments. This inner-city stretch ran about 43 km, past Bernauer Straße, the Brandenburg Gate, Potsdamer Platz, Checkpoint Charlie and the Spree. At least 140 people were killed at the Wall or died in connection with it, by the estimate of the Berlin Wall Memorial.

properties.name: Berlin Wall (outer ring)
properties.description: About 112 km of wall and fence cut West Berlin off from the East German countryside around it, following the old city boundary through forests, fields, lakes and villages. Like the inner-city Wall it began as barbed wire on 13 August 1961 and was strengthened over the years with concrete, a patrol road and watchtowers.

properties.name: Death strip
properties.description: Behind the front wall, on the East Berlin side, lay the death strip: raked sand, a patrol road, lamps, watchtowers, alarm fences and a second wall. Guards had orders to stop escapes, if need be by shooting. Houses along the border were emptied and pulled down to widen it.

properties.name: Berlin Wall after the opening
properties.description: On the night of 9 November 1989 crowds forced the crossings open after a confused announcement of new travel rules. Berliners climbed the Wall and chipped pieces off it, and new crossings were opened through it over the following weeks. Official demolition began on 13 June 1990.

properties.name: Tempelhof Airport
properties.description: West Berlin's main airport, in the American sector. The Soviets blockaded West Berlin from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949, and the Western Allies supplied it by air from 26 June 1948 until 30 September 1949. Some 2.3 million tonnes of food, coal and supplies were flown in, and more than 100 people died in accidents.

properties.name: RAF Gatow
properties.description: The Royal Air Force airfield in the British sector, on the western edge of the city. It was one of the three landing grounds of the Airlift, and RAF flying boats landed on the Havel nearby. The Wall ran along its western fence.

properties.name: Tegel airfield
properties.description: Built for the Airlift in the French sector by about 19,000 Berliners, many of them women, in roughly 90 days. It opened on 5 November 1948. In December the French blew up the masts of the Soviet-run radio station nearby, which stood in the way of the approach.

properties.name: Checkpoint Charlie
properties.description: The Allied checkpoint on Friedrichstraße, the crossing for foreigners and Allied staff between the American sector and East Berlin. On 27 and 28 October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other here for about 16 hours. The guard hut was lifted away on 22 June 1990.

properties.name: Where Peter Fechter died
properties.description: On 17 August 1962 East German guards shot 18-year-old Peter Fechter as he tried to climb the Wall on Zimmerstraße. He was left to bleed to death in the death strip in view of West Berliners, who could not reach him.

properties.name: Brandenburg Gate
properties.description: The 18th-century city gate stood just inside the Soviet sector. From August 1961 it was shut off behind the Wall, the symbol of the divided city. Ronald Reagan spoke in front of it on 12 June 1987, and it reopened to pedestrians on 22 December 1989.

properties.name: Reichstag (ruin)
properties.description: The old German parliament, burned in 1933 and wrecked in the battle for Berlin in 1945. It stood in the British sector, a few metres from the sector border. Its shattered dome was blown up in 1954.

properties.name: Reichstag
properties.description: Rebuilt in plain form without its dome from 1961, the Reichstag stood right beside the Wall. Because of Berlin's four-power status the West German parliament held no full sessions here; it housed an exhibition on German history and occasional committee meetings.

properties.name: Alexanderplatz
properties.description: The big square in the heart of East Berlin, rebuilt in the late 1960s as a showpiece of socialist planning. On 4 November 1989 it held the largest demonstration in East German history, with hundreds of thousands calling for free speech and reform.

properties.name: Fernsehturm (TV tower)
properties.description: East Berlin's television tower, 365 m tall, opened on 3 October 1969, just before the GDR's 20th anniversary. It was built to show off socialist progress and could be seen from all over West Berlin.

properties.name: Glienicke Bridge
properties.description: The bridge over the Havel between the American sector and Potsdam in East Germany, with the border across its middle. Closed to ordinary traffic after 1961, it was where the superpowers swapped captured agents. The first exchange, on 10 February 1962, traded the American U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers for the Soviet spy Rudolf Abel.

properties.name: Potsdamer Platz
properties.description: Before the war one of the busiest squares in Europe, where the American, British and Soviet sectors met. Bombed in the war, it was cut through by the Wall in 1961 and became an empty stretch of death strip. A new crossing opened here on 12 November 1989.

properties.name: Soviet War Memorial (Tiergarten)
properties.description: A memorial and cemetery for Soviet soldiers killed in the Battle of Berlin, unveiled on 11 November 1945. It stood in the British sector, but Soviet soldiers kept guard here throughout the Cold War.

properties.name: Rathaus Schöneberg
properties.description: The town hall that served as seat of West Berlin's government from 1948. On 26 June 1963 John F. Kennedy spoke here to a vast crowd and declared "Ich bin ein Berliner".

properties.name: Friedrichstraße station
properties.description: A station in East Berlin that became the main rail crossing between East and West. West Berlin's U-Bahn and S-Bahn trains passed under East Berlin through closed "ghost stations" but stopped here, where travellers could change trains or go through East German controls.

properties.name: Tränenpalast
properties.description: The "Palace of Tears", the glass departure hall at Friedrichstraße station for travellers going from East to West Berlin. It took its name from the farewells of East Berliners who could not follow their visitors west.

properties.name: Bornholmer Straße crossing
properties.description: A border crossing on the Bösebrücke between Prenzlauer Berg and Wedding. Late on 9 November 1989, with thousands pressing at the gate, the officer in charge opened it: the first crossing to open that night.

properties.name: Stasi headquarters
properties.description: Headquarters of the Ministry for State Security, the Stasi, East Germany's secret police, on Normannenstraße in Lichtenberg. The compound grew to dozens of buildings. On 15 January 1990 citizens stormed it to stop the destruction of files.

properties.name: Oberbaum Bridge
properties.description: A double-deck brick bridge over the Spree between Kreuzberg and Friedrichshain, open from 1963 to West Berlin pedestrians only. Between 1966 and 1975 five children from Kreuzberg drowned in the river here, because rescuers from the West were not allowed into East German water.

properties.name: Wall on Mühlenstraße
properties.description: Here the Spree was the border, and the Wall stood on the Friedrichshain bank along Mühlenstraße, facing East Berlin. Artists painted it in 1990, and about 1.3 km of it survives as the East Side Gallery.

properties.name: Bernauer Straße
properties.description: Here the border ran along the house fronts: the pavement lay in the French sector, the houses on the south side in the Soviet sector. In August 1961 residents jumped from their windows to the West, and Ida Siekmann died doing so on 22 August. Later escape tunnels ran under the street, among them Tunnel 57, which brought 57 people out in October 1964.
